characters: Ngede: a small brown-and-white honeyguide bird with a loud, chattering call.
Gingile: a strong young hunter with a spear and a bag, greedy and sure of himself.
The leopard: a large leopard asleep on the branch of a tree.

narrationPlan.voice: A warm storyteller, with a distinct voice for each character
narrationPlan.pace: Bright and easy, then sharp (about 125 words per minute)
notes: Read as a storyteller by the fire, with a distinct, natural voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each comprehension check so learners can reason first.
Pronounce the names of characters and places clearly, with respect for the languages they come from.

music: Quick, chattering flute over a light drum (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Where it is told: a tale of the Ndebele people of Zimbabwe and the Zulu people of South Africa. Similar stories are told wherever honeyguides and honey hunters work together.
A traditional tale retold in original words for Ghanaian JHS learners. It is not copied from any published version.

Science link: the greater honeyguide is a real bird that leads people to bees’ nests in several African countries and feeds on the wax left behind. It is one of the few wild animals known to work with people in this way.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated JHS age band (Basic 7 to Basic 9) and BECE conceptual level?
Is the tale retold with respect for the people it comes from, and is its lesson clear?
The names Ngede and Gingile follow the traditional telling; confirm spelling with a Zulu or Ndebele speaker.
Check that the fall is told without frightening detail.

teacherGuide.overview: A southern African tale about a honey hunter who cheats his guide, teaching gratitude and respect for custom, with a link to real animal behaviour.
learningGoals: Explain the partnership between the bird and the hunter.
Apply the lesson to thanking those who help us.

subjectLinks.subject: English Language (NaCCA CCP: reading, listening, and oral literature; codes to verify)
Social Studies (NaCCA CCP B9.3.3.1.1: Strand 3: Sense of Purpose, Sub-Strand 3: Culture and National Identity)
subjectLinks.link: Values: gratitude and respect for custom and nature

beforeReading: Ask: do you know of any wild animal that helps people? Tell learners there is a bird that does.
whileReading: Stop after Page 4. Ask: why has the bird come back?
afterReading: Learners list three people who help them and how each can be thanked.
discussion: Gingile said, “I climbed the tree. You only showed the way.” How much is showing the way worth?
reflection: Who has shown you the way to something good? Have you thanked them?

support: Play “follow the bird”: one learner calls and leads another to a hidden “honey” card.
stretch: Find out how honeyguides and people call to each other in Mozambique or Tanzania.
